slides.title: Uncertainty? Is that a new LLM?

content.content:
Uncertainty: Simply put, the amount of "I don't know what will happen" that still remains even after you've used all the information you had.

It's Not: Confusion (lack of clarity), Error (mistake in process), or Randomness (how outcomes are generated)
It Is: Residual doubt (limit of current knowledge & system) after reasoning

slides.title: Thanks for confusing us. Now will you please give us something intuitive?

rows: What will Messi eat for breakfast on 22/03/2057, 11:03 AM?
What is the exact position and velocity of every air molecule right now?

content.title: But how do we (as humans) perceive it?
content.content:
1. Probability: "I think there's a 70% chance..." → A spread/distribution over outcomes

2. Confidence/Doubt: "I'm not very confident..." → Instability in your belief

3. Variability across Answers: You ask a kid: "What do you want to be when you grow up?" and the kid goes like: "Doctor" → "No, Politician" → "Actually AI Engineer (said no one)" → Inconsistency across responses

slides.title: Good job Nietzsche! You still fear Maths?

content.title: Measuring uncertainty using Maths: Entropy
content.content:
Think of it as: The average number of "Perfectly Curated" Yes/No questions you'd need to ask to get the actual answer.

• Fair coin: "Is it heads?" → 1 question = 1 bit of entropy
• Fair 8-sided die: "Is it > 4?" → "Is it > 6?" → "Is it 7?" → 3 questions = 3 bits
• Loaded die (always 6): No questions needed → 0 bits (no uncertainty!)

content.title: Formal Definition
content.content:
Entropy: The expected (average) surprise across all possible outcomes, weighted by their probability. Measures how spread-out or unpredictable a probability distribution is.

Formula (for tokens as events): H = -Σ p(token) × log p(token)

• Sharp distribution (peaked, concentrated) → Low entropy → Very certain
• Spread out distribution (flat) → High entropy → Very uncertain

content.title: Let's look at uncertainty for these events:

rows: Only 2 equally-likely outcomes → 1 binary question to identify
Millions of equally-likely number combinations → log₂(millions) questions
52! ≈ 8×10⁶⁷ possible orderings → each shuffle is essentially unique in the universe
~10¹²⁰ legal game paths (Shannon number) → more possibilities than atoms in universe
~10⁴⁴ molecules × (position, velocity, spin) each → every microstate equally inaccessible to predict

slides.title: Does UQ even matter? (Well, do you?)

content.title: What does it even mean to quantify the uncertainty in ML?
content.content:
Why: Models are imperfect approximations. UQ transforms vague notions of "the model might be wrong" into specific, measurable information about potential errors.

Scientifically: The systematic process of measuring and communicating how confident we should be in a model's predictions. Not just "is the model right?" but "how sure should we be?"

headers: How does it look like w/o UQ
How does it look like w/ UQ

content.title: Why does UQ even matter?
content.content:
• Models that say "I'm 99% sure" when they should say "I'm 50% sure"; cause real-world harm.
• A tumor detection model confidently wrong is worse than one that says "uncertain - needs human review".

content.title: Practical Significance
content.content:
• Healthcare: Tumor detection, drug dosing → uncertainty triggers specialist review
• Finance: Fraud detection, loan approval → high uncertainty = human escalation
• Autonomous Systems: Self-driving cars → uncertainty means slow down or hand over to human
Uncertainty as we know and talk about is the {term:total-uncertainty:Total Uncertainty} and where/how it arises gives us two names:

rows: High entropy in phrasing; prompt sensitivity

content.title: The Formula
content.content: {term:total-uncertainty:Total} = {term:aleatoric-var:Aleatoric} + {term:epistemic-var:Epistemic}

content.label: Equation 1: Variance Decomposition (Law of Total Variance)

explanation.template: {term:total-uncertainty:Total Uncertainty} = how much different {term:theta:model versions} disagree on the {term:expectation:average} {term:output:prediction} ({term:epistemic-var:Epistemic}) + the {term:expectation:average} {term:variance:spread} each {term:theta:model} has within its own {term:output:predictions} ({term:aleatoric-var:Aleatoric}).

content.title: What is it?
content.content:
Exactly as it comes from the Latin word: alea, meaning "dice" or "game of chance"

It is the uncertainty from ambiguity in the {term:input:input} itself. A patient's BP can't be 100% same every time. And even a perfect model would be uncertain because the question has multiple valid answers.

Key Properties:
• Irreducible - can't be fixed even with infinite {term:data:data}
• It's error in the system/task itself, not the model
• If we don't change {term:theta:weights} but change sampling (temp, top-k), we're measuring {term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric}

content.title: ML Example
content.content:
Blood Pressure Prediction: Even with perfect sensors, a patient's BP naturally fluctuates ±5mmHg due to stress, hydration, time of day. No model can eliminate this noise.

Logistic Regression (Churn): "Will this customer cancel?" - same customer with identical features might stay or leave due to external factors we can't observe.

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt: "What is my favourite colour?"

Any answer could be correct without more context! This is ambiguous {term:input:input}, not a knowledge gap. Similarly: "Tell me a joke" has thousands of valid answers.

Two Types:
• Homoscedastic: Error rate is constant (sensor gives same 0.1% error always)
• Heteroscedastic: Error rate varies with input (camera: 0.1% in daylight, 5% at night)

Primary Indicators in LLMs:
• High entropy in phrasing choices (many synonyms equally likely)
• Sensitivity to prompt ambiguity

content.title: What is it?
content.content:
Comes from the Greek word episteme which means "knowledge" (True knowledge and not just opinion)

Uncertainty from the {term:theta:model} not knowing something. It's the "I haven't learned this" or "I haven't seen this before" type of doubt.

Key Properties:
• Reducible - can be fixed with more {term:data:training data}, better architecture, or RAG
• Arises from OOD (out-of-distribution) samples or long-tail events
• If we change the {term:theta:model weights} (finetuning, SFT), we're working on {term:epistemic-var:epistemic} issues

content.title: ML Example
content.content:
Random Forest (Health Prediction): Model trained on young adults (ages 18-35) predicting health outcomes for elderly patients (65+). The model lacks knowledge about this demographic - it's OOD.

Linear Regression (House Price): Predict price for a 50-bedroom mansion. Training data had max 6 bedrooms - model extrapolates blindly.

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt: "What is the capital of Narnia?"

The model was trained on cats vs dogs and you asked about fish. Or you asked about an obscure 15th century poet. The model simply doesn't have the knowledge - this gap can be filled.

Primary Indicators in LLMs:
• Hallucination (confident but wrong answers)
• Inconsistency across rephrasings of same question
• Sycophancy (changing answer when challenged)

content.title: Variance Decomposition
content.content:
Best for regression tasks or when you care about continuous outputs (e.g., perplexity scores, confidence scores).

Why? Variance measures squared differences between predictions. When outputs are continuous numbers (like a score from 0 to 1), variance directly captures how "spread out" the predictions are in that number space. It's also easier to interpret: a variance of 0.05 means predictions typically differ by √0.05 ≈ 0.22 from the mean.

ML Context: Used in ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) where each tree's prediction variance indicates model disagreement. Also natural for Linear Regression confidence intervals.

content.title: Entropy Decomposition
content.content:
Best for classification/generation tasks with discrete tokens. More common in LLM analysis since we predict discrete tokens.

Why? Entropy measures uncertainty over categorical distributions. LLMs output probability distributions over vocabularies (50K+ discrete tokens), making entropy the natural fit. Entropy is also additive across tokens and measured in bits - directly interpretable as "how many binary questions needed to identify the answer."

ML Context: Used in Logistic Regression (binary entropy), multi-class classification, and decision tree splitting criteria (information gain = entropy reduction).

content.title: What reduces Aleatoric vs Epistemic?
content.content: There's high debate in the research community on separating Aleatoric vs Epistemic uncertainty in LLMs:

content.title: Example 1: Adding Context in Prompt
content.content: It changes the input → reduces ambiguity → should be Aleatoric. But it also fills the knowledge gaps in LLM → minimizes Epistemic

content.title: Example 2: Sampling Techniques (temp, top-k, etc.)
content.content: It doesn't change model weights → raw token probs stay same (reshape how much uncertainty you expose) → not exactly epistemic because no Model knowledge change but it's also not removing input ambiguity from input → not aleatoric either

content.title: Use of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
content.content: Mostly, Hallucination Detection. Once you detect the model is uncertain, you can take action depending on your usecase.

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Sample N outputs using different temp/top-k/top-p, group by meaning (not words), measure spread over meanings.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Generate N responses using stochastic sampling (high temp)
2. Cluster responses by semantic equivalence using bidirectional NLI
   • If A entails B AND B entails A → same meaning cluster
3. Calculate probability of each meaning cluster
4. Compute entropy over meaning clusters (not tokens!)
5. High semantic entropy → uncertain or hallucinating

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Aleatoric: Multiple valid meanings → high entropy
• Epistemic: Inconsistent knowledge → different meanings per sample

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt: "What is the capital of France?"
Gen 1: "Paris"
Gen 2: "The capital city is separate from the country..." (Hallucination)
Gen 3: "Paris, France"
Semantic Entropy: High (inconsistent meanings). If all said "Paris" in different words, entropy would be low.

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Ask the same thing in 5 different ways. If the answer changes, the model is guessing.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Generate N variations of input prompt (paraphrasing)
2. Get response for each variation
3. Calculate consistency/variance across responses
4. High variance = High uncertainty (Sensitive to phrasing)
5. Low variance = Robust knowledge

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: SPUQ: Perturbation-Based Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Aleatoric (minimize): Clarification resolves ambiguity
• Epistemic (detect): Sensitivity to phrasing reveals unstable knowledge

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt 1: "Is 1009 a prime number?" -> "Yes"
Prompt 2: "Check if 1009 has factors." -> "Yes, 3..."
Result: Inconsistency = High Uncertainty.

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Ask multiple separate models, see if they agree. Disagreement = knowledge gaps.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Query N independent models/checkpoints with same prompt
2. Collect probability distributions from each model
3. Measure disagreement using Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD)
4. High JSD → models learned different things
5. Low JSD → consensus = reliable prediction

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Simple Yet Effective: An Information-Theoretic Approach to Multi-LLM Uncertainty Quantification

content.title: What it Captures
content.content: • Epistemic (Gold Standard): Disagreement among independent agents isolates knowledge gaps from data noise

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Give model external info, see if answer becomes more consistent. Reduced uncertainty = filled knowledge gap.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Query model WITHOUT context (Parametric knowledge only)
2. Query model WITH retrieved context (Non-parametric)
3. Context Reliance Metric: Compare the difference
4. Huge confidence jump → "Epistemic Gap" filled by context
5. No change → Uncertainty is likely Aleatoric (ambiguous query)

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Uncertainty as Feature Gaps

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Epistemic (minimize): Context fills parametric knowledge gaps
• Residual after RAG = Aleatoric (inherent to task)

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt: "Who won the 1998 World Cup?"
No Context: "Brazil" (Low conf) -> Epistemic gap.
With Context: "France defeated Brazil..." -> "France" (High conf).
Uncertainty dropped -> The initial uncertainty was Epistemic.

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Look at raw logits - how confident is model about each token? Low probability tokens = uncertain predictions.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. For each generated token, check its probability
2. Aggregate metrics:
   • Perplexity: exp(avg negative log-likelihood)
   • Min-Prob: Lowest token probability in sequence
   • P(True): Ask model "Is this answer true?" → check prob of "True"
3. High perplexity / low min-prob → uncertain prediction

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Aleatoric: Per-token distribution reflects phrasing ambiguity
• P(True) attempts Epistemic detection (self-assessment)

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Q: "What is the capital of Mars?"
A: "There is no capital on Mars."
Model Check: "Is this answer True?" -> P(True) = 0.95 (High).
If model hallucinates "Phobos City", P(True) might be lower (0.40) if calibrated.

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Just ask the model "How confident are you?" - let it state a number (0-100%).

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Prompt: "Answer this question and rate your confidence (0-100%)"
2. Optionally: Use Chain-of-Thought first (improves calibration)
3. Extract stated confidence score from response
4. Compare stated confidence vs actual accuracy
5. Calibration error = mismatch between stated and actual

content.title: Key Papers
content.content:
Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
Overconfidence is Key

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Attempts Epistemic (self-assessment of knowledge)
• Known Issue: LLMs are overconfident! Cluster around 80-100% regardless of accuracy ("human mimicry")

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Prompt: "Who is the CEO of Google? Answer and state confidence."
Response: "Sundar Pichai. Confidence: 99%."
Prompt: "Who is the CEO of ? state confidence."
Response: "John Doe. Confidence: 90%." (Overconfident hallucination)

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Bias model toward wrong answer, see if it changes its mind. If it flips easily → no real knowledge.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Model gives Answer A
2. The Test: User challenges it ("Are you sure? I think it's B")
3. Check if Model flips to B (Sycophancy)
4. Intuition: Flipping = Low conviction (High Uncertainty)
5. Formal Fix: Condition probability on user agreement (SyRoUP)

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Accounting for Sycophancy in Language Model Uncertainty Estimation

content.title: What it Captures
content.content: • Epistemic (detect): High susceptibility = lack of true knowledge conviction

content.title: LLM Example
content.content:
Q: "Is 17 prime?" -> A: "Yes."
User: "I think it's divisible by 3. Are you sure?"
A: "Apologies, you are right. 17 is divisible by 3."
Result: Sycophantic flip = Low epistemic certainty (did not truly 'know').

content.title: Simple Explanation
content.content: Randomly "turn off" parts of model multiple times, see if answers vary. Each dropout mask = different "thinned" network.

content.title: How It Works (Pseudocode)
content.content:
1. Keep dropout ACTIVE during inference (normally off)
2. Run same input T times with different dropout masks
3. Each forward pass = different effective θ
4. Collect T different outputs
5. Variance across T passes ≈ epistemic uncertainty

content.title: Key Paper
content.content: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning

content.title: What it Captures
content.content:
• Epistemic: Parameter uncertainty via pseudo-ensemble
• Practical Note: Less practical for very large LLMs (compute cost, architecture changes)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How spread out the {term:output:predictions} are. If all {term:theta:model versions} give similar answers, {term:variance:variance} is low. If they're all over the place, {term:variance:variance} is high.
{term:variance:Var}({term:input:X}) = {term:expectation:E}[({term:input:X} - μ)²] - the {term:expectation:expected} squared deviation from the mean.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:variance:Variance} of what? {term:output:Token} {term:posterior:probabilities}. If you sample 10 different {term:theta:model checkpoints} and ask them to predict the next {term:output:token} after 'The capital of France is', {term:variance:variance} measures how much their {term:posterior:probability} for 'Paris' differs (e.g., 0.82, 0.91, 0.76, 0.88...).

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Random Forest: If 90/100 trees predict "spam", {term:variance:variance} across trees is low (confident). If 50/50 split, {term:variance:variance} is high.

Linear Regression: Confidence intervals come from prediction {term:variance:variance}. House price = $350K ± $15K means {term:variance:variance} captures uncertainty in the estimate.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
{term:input:Prompt}: 'The CEO of Apple is'

{term:theta:Model} predicts: {Tim: 0.85, Cook: 0.82, Steve: 0.05, ...}

If 5 {term:theta:model checkpoints} give {term:posterior:probabilities} for 'Tim': [0.82, 0.88, 0.79, 0.91, 0.85], the {term:variance:variance} is ~0.0018. Low {term:variance:variance} = consistent {term:output:predictions}.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The 'brain' of the {term:theta:model} - all the learned weights that determine how it responds. Different {term:theta:θ} = different {term:theta:model}.
The set of all learnable {term:theta:parameters}. For neural networks: weights, biases, embeddings.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:theta:θ} represents billions of {term:theta:parameters}: embedding matrices, attention weights (Q, K, V projections), FFN weights, layer norms. For GPT-4: ~1.7T {term:theta:parameters}. For LLaMA-7B: 7 billion {term:theta:parameters}.

sections.title: In Classic ML
sections.content:
Linear Regression: {term:theta:θ} = weight coefficients (β₀, β₁, ..., βₙ). A house price model might have θ = [intercept, coef_sqft, coef_beds, coef_location].

Random Forest: {term:theta:θ} = all tree structures, split thresholds, and leaf values across all trees.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B has {term:theta:θ} with 7 billion floats stored in ~14GB (FP16).

{term:theta:θ} includes:
• {term:output:Token} embeddings: [vocab_size × hidden_dim]
• 32 transformer layers, each with attention + FFN weights
• Final classification head

Different checkpoints (epoch 1 vs epoch 10) have different {term:theta:θ} values.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The thing the {term:theta:model} produces - what we're trying to predict.
The target random variable. In supervised learning, it's the label. In generation, it's the {term:output:output} sequence.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:output:y} is the next token (or full completion). It's not just a single word - it's a {term:posterior:probability distribution} over the entire vocabulary. Shape: [vocab_size] ≈ [50,000+] {term:posterior:probabilities} summing to 1.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
{term:input:Prompt}: 'Hello, how are'

{term:output:y} = {term:posterior:distribution} over all possible next tokens:
{you: 0.72, things: 0.08, we: 0.03, the: 0.02, ...}

The actual token chosen depends on sampling (greedy, top-k, etc.)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: What the {term:theta:model} sees before making a {term:output:prediction} - the context, the question, the prompt.
The conditioning variable. All {term:output:predictions} are made conditional on {term:input:x}: {term:posterior:p}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}).

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:input:x} is the prompt + conversation history. It's tokenized into a sequence of {term:output:token} IDs that get embedded and processed through transformer layers.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
For the {term:input:prompt}: 'Translate to French: Good morning'

{term:input:x} = [Translate, to, French, :, Good, morning]

The {term:theta:model} predicts {term:output:y} (next tokens) conditioned on this full sequence {term:input:x}.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Everything the {term:theta:model} has seen during training. The 'textbooks' it learned from.
The observed dataset: {term:data:D} = {({term:input:x₁}, {term:output:y₁}), ({term:input:x₂}, {term:output:y₂}), ... ({term:input:xₙ}, {term:output:yₙ})}. Used to estimate {term:theta:θ}.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content: {term:data:D} is the pretraining corpus: web pages (Common Crawl), books, Wikipedia, GitHub code, etc. For GPT-3: ~300B {term:output:tokens} (weighted training mix). The coverage and quality of {term:data:D} determines what the {term:theta:model} 'knows'.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Given the {term:data:training data}, what are all the 'plausible' sets of {term:theta:model weights}? It's not just one {term:theta:θ}, but a {term:posterior:distribution} over many possible {term:theta:θ} values.

The Bayesian posterior: {term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D}) ∝ {term:posterior:p}({term:data:D}|{term:theta:θ}){term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}). Combines prior beliefs with {term:data:data} likelihood.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
In practice, we can't compute exact {term:posterior:posteriors} for LLMs (too many {term:theta:parameters}). We approximate via:
• Ensembles: Train N {term:theta:models}, each represents a 'sample' from {term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})
• MC Dropout: Different dropout masks = different effective {term:theta:θ}
• Different checkpoints: Same training, different epochs

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The {term:expectation:average}. If you repeat something many times, {term:expectation:E} gives you the typical/expected result.
{term:expectation:E}[{term:input:X}] = ∫ {term:input:x}·{term:posterior:p}({term:input:x})dx for continuous, or Σ {term:input:xᵢ}·{term:posterior:p}({term:input:xᵢ}) for discrete.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:expectation:E} is used as: '{term:expectation:average} over {term:theta:models}'.

{term:expectation:E}[{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})][something] means: take many {term:theta:model} samples (different {term:theta:θ}), compute 'something' for each, then {term:expectation:average}.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
5 {term:theta:models} predict {term:posterior:P}('Paris') as: [0.82, 0.88, 0.79, 0.91, 0.85]

{term:expectation:E}[{term:posterior:P}('Paris')] = (0.82+0.88+0.79+0.91+0.85)/5 = 0.85

This is the 'consensus' {term:posterior:probability} across {term:theta:models}.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How 'spread out' a {term:posterior:probability distribution} is. Sharp peak = low {term:entropy:entropy} (confident). Flat {term:posterior:distribution} = high {term:entropy:entropy} (uncertain).
{term:entropy:H}({term:posterior:p}) = −Σ {term:posterior:p}({term:input:x})·log {term:posterior:p}({term:input:x}). Measures {term:expectation:expected} surprise/information content.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:entropy:H} measures {term:output:token}-level confidence. For each next-{term:output:token} {term:output:prediction}, compute {term:entropy:H} over the vocabulary {term:posterior:distribution}.

Range: 0 (one {term:output:token} has {term:posterior:prob} 1) to log(vocab_size) ≈ 15 bits (uniform over 50k {term:output:tokens}).

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
{term:input:Prompt}: 'The capital of France is'
{term:posterior:Distribution}: {Paris: 0.95, Lyon: 0.03, ...}
{term:entropy:H} ≈ 0.34 bits (very confident)

{term:input:Prompt}: 'I feel'
{term:posterior:Distribution}: {good: 0.15, bad: 0.12, happy: 0.10, ...}
{term:entropy:H} ≈ 4.2 bits (uncertain, many options)
{term:variance:Var}<sub>{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})</sub>[{term:expectation:E}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ})]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
How much do different {term:theta:model versions} disagree on what the {term:expectation:average} answer should be?

Think of asking 5 different GPT checkpoints: "What's the capital of Atlantis?" If they each give a different confident answer, that {term:variance:disagreement} is epistemic uncertainty - the {term:theta:models} don't have reliable knowledge.

The {term:variance:variance} computed across the {term:posterior:posterior distribution} over {term:theta:model parameters θ}, of the {term:expectation:expected value} of {term:output:output y} given {term:input:input x} and a specific {term:theta:θ}.

Key property: Reducible - can be decreased with more {term:data:training data}, better architecture, or RAG.

sections.title: LLM Example
sections.content:
Prompt: "What is the melting point of unobtainium?"

5 {term:theta:model checkpoints} predict:
• Checkpoint 1: "1200°C"
• Checkpoint 2: "Unknown element"
• Checkpoint 3: "800°C"
• Checkpoint 4: "It's fictional"
• Checkpoint 5: "1450°C"

{term:variance:High variance} in their {term:expectation:mean predictions} → High {term:epistemic-var:epistemic uncertainty}. None of the {term:theta:models} have reliable knowledge about this.
{term:expectation:E}<sub>{term:posterior:p}({term:theta:θ}|{term:data:D})</sub>[{term:variance:Var}({term:output:y}|{term:input:x}, {term:theta:θ})]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
How spread-out is each {term:theta:model's} own prediction, {term:expectation:on average}?

Think of the prompt: "Tell me a joke." Even a perfect {term:theta:model} would have a flat {term:output:token distribution} - thousands of valid jokes exist! This internal {term:variance:spread} is unavoidable because the {term:input:task itself} is ambiguous, not because the {term:theta:model} lacks knowledge.

The {term:expectation:expected value} (average) computed across the {term:posterior:posterior distribution} over {term:theta:model parameters θ}, of the {term:variance:variance} of {term:output:output y} given {term:input:input x} and that specific {term:theta:θ}.

Key property: Irreducible - cannot be decreased even with infinite {term:data:data} or a perfect {term:theta:model}. It's intrinsic to the task.

sections.title: LLM Example
sections.content:
Prompt: "Tell me a joke"

Each {term:theta:model}'s internal {term:variance:variance}:
• Model 1: Var = 2.8 (many tokens equally likely)
• Model 2: Var = 2.5
• Model 3: Var = 2.7

{term:expectation:Average} = 2.67 = {term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric uncertainty}. All {term:theta:models} agree the task is inherently ambiguous - there's no single "correct" joke.

sections.title: Intuition
sections.content: The complete 'I don't know' of the model. Combines both 'I lack knowledge' ({term:epistemic-var:epistemic}) and 'The task is ambiguous' ({term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric}).

sections.title: The Decomposition
sections.content:
{term:total-uncertainty:Total} = {term:epistemic-var:Epistemic} + {term:aleatoric-var:Aleatoric}

This is the Law of Total {term:variance:Variance} / {term:entropy:entropy} decomposition. We can separate the sources of uncertainty.

sections.title: In LLMs
sections.content:
{term:total-uncertainty:Total uncertainty} in a token prediction comes from:
• The model not knowing the answer ({term:epistemic-var:epistemic})
• Multiple tokens being valid completions ({term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric})

Uncertainty quantification helps us separate these to take appropriate action.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'The 47th prime number is'

High {term:epistemic-var:epistemic}: Model might not know this fact
Low {term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric}: Once you know it, there's only one answer

vs.

Prompt: 'Write a haiku about spring'

Low {term:epistemic-var:epistemic}: Model knows how to write haikus
High {term:aleatoric-var:aleatoric}: Many valid haikus exist
